clue.text: Sky will do play-off and cricket finals

indicators.note: the finals of these four words are their closing letters, read in order

explanation.surface: A broadcaster promises to show the play-off and the cricket finals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sky' looks like the satellite broadcaster in a sports surface, but it is a verb, to hit the ball high.
explanation.definitionFit: To sky a ball in cricket or golf is to hit it high into the air, the same as lofting it.

clue.text: Theorem I talk up captivates old bishop

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the captured run reads from bottom to top
the words Theorem I talk hold the answer captive inside them

explanation.surface: A mathematician's chatter about a theorem enthrals an elderly churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivates' signals letters held inside THEOREM I TALK, and 'up' turns them: KLATIMEROEHT reversed contains the run.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Latimer was a sixteenth-century Bishop of Worcester burned as a Protestant martyr in Oxford.

clue.text: Disapprove of father that hurt sister shielding naval officer

parts.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
ow is the exclamation one makes when something hurts

indicators.note: the nun shields, so she stands round the officer

parts.note: a sister in religion is a nun
PO is a petty officer in the navy

explanation.surface: A priest's injured sister protects a sailor, and he frowns on the whole affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that hurt' stands for the cry of pain itself; 'shielding' has the sister wrapped protectively round the naval officer.
explanation.definitionFit: To regard something with disfavour is to look on it with a disapproving scowl.

clue.text: Roman Bath that is as usual heaving, without question

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the scrambled letters go round the next piece
heaving suggests a churning, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is' (id est)

explanation.surface: The Roman baths are packed as ever, and nobody asks why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, so the scrambled letters surround the question. Aquae Sulis was the Roman name for the English city of Bath.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquae Sulis, 'waters of Sulis', was the name of the Roman spa town now called Bath in Somerset.

clue.text: Borough promotes man on board

definitions.meaning: one of the five administrative districts of New York City
in chess a pawn reaching the far rank is promoted, usually to the most powerful piece

explanation.surface: A town council advances a member of its board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man on board' looks like a committee member, but it is a chess piece, here a pawn being promoted.
explanation.definitionFit: Queens is a New York borough; in chess, to queen a pawn is to promote it on the eighth rank.

clue.text: A row about Parisian who's recalling great winger

indicators.note: the row goes about, so A LINE surrounds the French word

parts.note: a row of things is a line
qui is French for who, as a Parisian would say it

explanation.surface: Somebody from Paris starts a quarrel and reminds us of a great footballer on the wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' wants to be a quarrel; it is a line. 'about' wraps A and the row round the French word; the 's of who's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquiline means eagle-like, as of a hooked nose, so it recalls that great bird of prey.

clue.text: One giving order to land on Red Square (name withheld)?

definitions.text: One giving order to land on Red Square (name withheld)?

indicators.note: the clue's letters are given a new order, so they are rearranged
a withheld item is kept back, so that letter is taken out

explanation.surface: An RAF officer orders his pilots to touch down in Moscow's famous square, his identity kept secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one N ('name withheld') from LAND ON RED SQUARE and 'giving order to' rearranges the remaining fourteen letters. As a whole the clue pictures an officer commanding a landing.
explanation.definitionFit: An RAF squadron leader commands a squadron of aircraft and so issues orders, including landing instructions.

clue.text: Lily aims at serving regulars and one from the Wool Pack

indicators.note: regular letters are every other one, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A barmaid called Lily aims to serve the regular customers at the Woolpack pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The Woolpack is the pub in the British TV soap Emmerdale, so 'regulars' looks like its drinkers; here it picks alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A llama is a South American animal kept for its wool, so a member of a woolly herd.

clue.text: Male and female below stage

indicators.note: in a down clue, the female word sits below the stage word

parts.note: a step is a stage in a process
a hen is a female bird

explanation.surface: A man and a woman are positioned beneath a theatre stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male and female' reads as a pair, but 'Male' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen is a man's first name, so it is an example of a male.

clue.text: Expecting folks to stop being obstructive

indicators.note: the relatives plug the gap, sitting inside the obstructive phrase

parts.note: something obstructive is in the way
one's folks are one's family

explanation.surface: Someone hopes the relatives will quit getting in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expecting' looks like a verb of hoping, but it means pregnant; 'to stop' has the relatives plugging the obstructive phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To be expecting is to be pregnant, euphemistically said to be carrying a baby.

clue.text: Easily best time had by Queen going to Oz

parts.note: R is for Regina, Latin for queen
oz is the abbreviation for ounce

explanation.surface: A monarch's trip to Australia ends with an easy victory over the locals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' looks like Australia, but it is the weight abbreviation, ounce.
explanation.definitionFit: To trounce an opponent is to beat them decisively and with ease.

clue.text: Keen to repeat until gutted and annoyed

indicators.note: the remaining pair is said twice over
the word until has its insides removed, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: to ate is to annoy or eat away at someone, as in what's eating you

explanation.surface: An eager person wants to go over things again until they become fed up and angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like an adjective (eager); it is the verb, to wail in mourning. 'gutted' leaves UL from UNTIL, and 'to repeat' doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: To keen is to wail in grief, and to ululate is to howl or wail.

clue.text: People rejoicing with composer gathering on outskirts of Czech city

indicators.note: the people gather other letters in among them

parts.note: men are people

indicators.note: the outskirts are the outside letters of the word Czech

parts.note: someone rejoicing is glad
J S Bach, the German composer

explanation.surface: Happy crowds and a famous composer assemble on the edge of a Czech town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Czech city' looks like a single phrase, but the city is German; 'gathering' has the people take in ON and the Czech outskirts.
explanation.definitionFit: Mönchengladbach is a German city in North Rhine-Westphalia, home to a well-known football club.

clue.text: Do letters expressing wish for one late start

parts.words: letters expressing wish for one late
parts.note: RIP, rest in peace, is the wish carved for someone who has died
off is the start of a race, as in 'they're off'

explanation.surface: A tardy guest is wished away in a letter just as things begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one late' means someone dead, not someone tardy.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone is slang for cheating them, and a swindle is a con.

clue.text: European who's raced ending with gold

parts.note: and joins things together as with does
or is gold in heraldry
ran is the past tense of run, a synonym of raced, placed last

explanation.surface: A Continental runner finishing with a gold medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' puts RAN last; 'who's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An Andorran comes from Andorra, the small Pyrenean state between France and Spain.

clue.text: Enjoy or get engaged in bawdy opera

indicators.note: the enjoyment words are held inside the bawdy word

parts.note: bawdy humour is rude
to dig something is slang for enjoying it

explanation.surface: Have fun and join in a ribald show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engaged in' has the bawdy word holding the enjoyment and 'or'. The opera is by Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruddigore is an 1887 comic operetta by Gilbert and Sullivan.

clue.text: Sort of acid scale descending to one hundred

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading downward the scale word comes before the numbers

parts.note: tartar is the hard scale that forms on teeth
I is the Roman numeral for one
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A musical scale runs down to a single note out of a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scale' suggests music or weighing; it is the deposit on teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartaric acid is an organic acid found in grapes and used in baking powder.

clue.text: Fertiliser's black I spread

parts.note: B is the pencil abbreviation for black
I as a number is one
a spread is a lavish meal

explanation.surface: A gardener scatters a dark fertiliser over the beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like a verb of scattering; it is a noun, a feast.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonemeal is ground animal bone, used as a slow-release garden fertiliser.

clue.text: Save high-tension jack up in place of washer

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the whole string reads from bottom to top

parts.note: save in the sense of except, which is but
HT is the abbreviation for high-tension
a jack is a sailor, and AB is an able seaman

explanation.surface: Someone tries to rescue a high-voltage jack-up instead of fixing the washing machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses BUT, HT and AB together: BUTHTAB read upward. 'washer' looks like a machine or a ring, but it is a person washing.
explanation.definitionFit: A bath is where a person sits to wash, so it is the place for someone bathing.

clue.text: Soften, squeezing down at the front until even

indicators.note: the softening word squeezes another letter inside it

parts.note: to allay pain is to soften it

indicators.note: the front of the word down is its first letter

explanation.surface: Feathers press down on the front until they are level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'even' looks like level, but it is a poetic word for evening.
explanation.definitionFit: All day lasts from morning right through to evening, the old poetic word being even.

clue.text: OK overtaking people I race round Gulf

indicators.note: the agreeing word takes in the others, surrounding them

parts.note: yes means OK, an agreement
men are people

explanation.surface: With approval I overtake other runners in a race around the bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'race' looks like a contest; it means a people. 'overtaking' has the agreement word take in the people and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Yemenis are the people of Yemen, a nation on the Arabian Peninsula bordering the Gulf of Aden.

clue.text: Show resentment reading news of rail strike once?

parts.note: BR was British Rail, the national railway before privatisation
workers on strike are idle

explanation.surface: Commuters bristle at news headlines of a former railway walkout.
explanation.walkthrough: A headline from the past reading 'BR idle' would announce a British Rail strike; 'once' marks BR as defunct, and 'reading news of' frames it as a headline.
explanation.definitionFit: To bridle is to take offence, like a horse pulling back its head against the reins.

clue.text: Limitation as art is savaged in Stalin's system

indicators.note: savaged words are torn apart and reassembled in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Under Stalin's regime, art was crushed by restrictions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'savaged' rearranges LIMITATION, AS and ART; 'is' joins them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Totalitarianism is a system of absolute state control, the kind of government Stalin imposed on the Soviet Union.

clue.text: Mistaken to rely on abandoning eastern European region

indicators.note: mistaken words are wrongly arranged, so the letters are reordered
abandoning means the letter for eastern is left out

explanation.surface: It is a mistake to depend on leaving the East for Central Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the E from TO RELY ('abandoning eastern') and 'Mistaken' rearranges TORLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyrol is an Alpine region straddling western Austria and northern Italy.

clue.text: Scrap that's done for a patch

definitions.text: Scrap that's done for a patch

parts.words: Scrap that's done for a patch
parts.note: a fight is waged over a patch of territory, as gangs fight over their area; patch also suggests a mending scrap of cloth

explanation.surface: A leftover bit of fabric gets used up to mend a hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' and 'patch' suggest sewing; the scrap is a fight and the patch a territory.
explanation.definitionFit: A territorial dispute between rival gangs or groups is a fight over their patch.

clue.text: Held that English is in decline

indicators.note: the English letter is put inside the holding phrase

parts.note: held means owned, which can be put as did own

explanation.surface: Someone maintained that English is going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held that' looks like 'maintained'; 'Held' is DID OWN, which 'is in' opens to take E.
explanation.definitionFit: To die down is to fade or subside, losing strength gradually.

clue.text: Had grouse ——- and there was indigestion!

definitions.meaning: to grouse is to grumble, so this means complained

explanation.surface: Someone ate game bird for dinner and was rewarded with a stomach upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grouse' looks like the game bird eaten at dinner, but it is a grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To grouse or complain is slang for griping, and an aching stomach is what indigestion brings.

clue.text: Short account in which one saved tragic heroine

indicators.note: short means the account's name is cut off at the end

parts.note: TESSA was a Tax-Exempt Special Savings Account, a British savings scheme of the 1990s

explanation.surface: A brief tale in which a tragic heroine is rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short account' looks like a brief story; it is a savings account clipped. Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Thomas Hardy's tragic heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Tess Durbeyfield is the doomed central character of Thomas Hardy's novel Tess of the d'Urbervilles.
